full_judgment:
Md Abdul Karim J: This Rule under Order 47, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of plaintiffs-appellants was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the Judgment and decree dated 12th April, 1994, passed by a Division Bench of this Court in First Appeal No. 184 of 1990 should not be reviewed and/or such other order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Original plaintiff Asaduzzaman filed Title Suit No. 101 of 1973 of the 4th court of learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, (subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 107 of 1988 of the 3rd Court of learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka) against defendant No. 1 A Satter Solaiman for specific performance of contract. Plaintiff Asaduzzaman died on 8-12-1991 (after dismissal of the suit on 9-6-1990). The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that defendant No. l A. Satter Solaiman, admittedly a non-Bengali national, executed an agreement on 14-10-1971 for sale of the suit property to the plaintiff at a consideration of taka one lac and bainapatra (Ext. 1) was executed by A Satter Solaiman on 14-10-1971 on receipt of Taka 75,000.00 as earnest money. It was stipulated that A Sattar Solaiman would execute and register the sale deed in favour of plaintiff Asaduzzaman. It is the case of the plaintiff that A Satter Solaiman delivered possession of the property in his favour on 14-10-1971. A deed of sale having not been executed and registered by A Satter Solaiman, the plaintiff was obliged to file the suit for specific performance of contract. In the written statements defendant No.2 Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and defendant No.3 Giasuddin Ahmed, claiming to be a lessee from the Government, denied the existence of any agreement for sale of the suit property contending that A Satter Solaiman left the then East Pakistan long before execution of the alleged agreement for sale of the suit property. The written statements claimed that the agreement for sale was a forged and fabricated document created for filing a suit for specific performance of contract. Subsequently the written statement of defendant No 1 A Salter Solaiman was struck off by the court, because the power of Attorney of the defendant had not been validated in Bangladesh and the written statement of defendant No.3 was also struck off on 24-6-1975 on the expiry of his lease. Before the trial Court as many as two witnesses were examined by the plaintiff as against none by the defendant. The trial Court dismissed the suit for failure of the plaintiff to prove due execution of the bainapatra and the Judgment and decree of the court below was upheld by a Division Bench of this court in First Appeal No. 184 of 1990. The trial Court held that the plaintiff could not prove writing of the documentby the scribe and that the plaintiff also did not examine the two attesting witnesses, Abdul Karim and Abdul Latif, and further that it was hardly believable that PW 1 Halima Jaman, wife of Asaduzzaman, and PW 2 Md Shajahan, a cousin of PW 1 were present in the house of defendant No. 1 at the time of execution of the document inasmuch as there was no attestation of the said agreement by these two witnesses. In other words, the suit was dismissed by the trial Court and the Judgment was upheld by a Division Bench of this court on the failure of the plaintiff to prove due execution of the deed of agreement. The present application under Order 47, rule 1 of the CPC for review of the Judgment passed in First Appeal No. 184 of 1990 has been submitted mainly on the ground of death of A Satter Solaiman on 10-12-1973. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court on 9-6-1990 and the First Appeal against the Judgment and decree of dismissal was dismissed on 12-4-1994. 

 4. Tile Division Bench presided over by his Lordship Anwarul Haque Chowdhury, J dismissed   the appeal being First Appeal No. 184 of 1990 on 12th April, 1994, affirming the Judgment and decree of the court below. In the Judgment the Division Bench mentions as follows: "It is not in evidence that the document was executed sitting in the house of the plaintiff where the wife would have lived but in the 	house of defendant No. I, namely, Abdus Satter Solaiman where the presence of both the wife of the plaintiff hi the house of Abdus Satter Solaiman and of PW 2, his brother-in-law would be not be Very normal and natural in the facts and circumstances of the case, they having 	not even been named as witnesses, but if present, ought to have been named as witnesses. No wonder the court below considered them to be procured witnesses. This finding of fact we do not consider to be arbitrary or an absurdity that could not be arrived at by a man of ordinary prudence in the facts and circumstances of the case. In the instant case PW 1 and PW 2 are close relations. They are interested people and the fact that they were present at the time of execution of the deed by Abdus Satter Solaiman, who is not before the court to admit execution of the document, and when also the abandoned property authority, namely, defendant No.2 is also not in court to admit the genuineness of the document is not proved without any independent corroboration of the same or any corroboration from the subsequent conduct of the executor." 

 5. It is submitted by Mr Khandakar Mahabubuddin Ahmed that the Division Bench hearing the First Appeal was influenced by "the facts and circumstances of the case", which remained in the back of the mind of the learned Judges. It is to meet "the facts and circumstances of the case" situation that the present review application has been filed with a prayer to set aside the Judgment and decree dated the 12th April, 1994, passed by the Division Bench in First Appeal No. 184 of 1990 and restore the first appeal and allow the petitioners to put in the death certificate of Abdus Satter Solaiman as additional evidence under Order 41, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 6. Order XL VII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as follows: "1. (1) Any person considering himself aggrieved (a) by a decree or order from which an appeal.is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred, (b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed, or (c) by a decision on reference from a Court of Small Causes, and who, from the discovery of new and important matter or evidence which, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed or order made, or on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face of the record, or for any other sufficient reason, desires to obtain a review of the decree passed or order made against him, may apply for a review of Judgment to the court which passed the decree or made the order." 

 7. Order XL VII, rule I, permits review of the Judgment on the ground of discovery of new and important matter or evidence which after the exercise of due diligence, was not within the knowledge of the petitioner or could not be produced by him at the time when the decree was passed or ordered. 

 10. The question is: Does the death certificate of Abdus Satter Solaiman indicating his death on 10-12-1'973 have a material bearing on the merit of the case? In the instant case the bainapatra (Ext 1) appears to have been attested by Abdul Karim and Abdul Latif. The evidence of PW 1 Halima Jaman, wife of Asaduzzaman, is that Abdul Latif is not traceable and that at time of execution of the bainapatra, defendant's lawyer, Mr Bakar, his clerk, Abdus Salter, and plaintiffs friend, Tahinu Saheb, were present It appears from the evidence of PW 1 that Abdul Latif was not traceable, Mr Baker is dead and his clerk, Abdul Satter, was also not traceable and Tahinus Saheb is also dead. There is, however, no explanation as to why Abdul Karim, one of the attesting witnesses, was not examined in the trial Court. There is no evidence that the witnesses examined were acquainted with the handwriting of the scribe. The trial Court found that PW 1 Halima Taman, wife of Asaduzzaman, and her cousin, PW 2 Md Shahjahan, are interested witnesses and the court disbelieved them, because their names did not appear in the deed of agreement as attesting witnesses. In other words, the trial Court dismissed the suit for failure of the plaintiff to prove due execution of the bainapatra and the Judgment and decree was affirmed by the Division Bench' in the First Appeal. It is, therefore, clear that the fact whether Abdus Satter Solaiman was alive or dead could not have any material bearing on the merit of the suit. So, the argument of Mr Khandakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed that the death certificate would have altered the facts and circumstances situation of the case in the mind of the learned Judges of the Division Bench does not appear to be convincing inasmuch as the dismissal of the suit by the Court below and also by the appellate Court rests on merit of the case.' It is clear that the certificate of death of the defendant obtained by heirs of Asaduzzaman after dismissal of the suit on merit by the trial court and the Court of appeal is not a new and important matter or evidence having any material bearing on the merit of the suit and, as such, it cannot be a ground for review of the Judgment under Order XLVII, rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code.
